title: Mars Exploration Portable Life Support System Schematic Study: Architecture Down-Selection

Mars Exploration Portable Life Support System Schematic Study: Architecture Down-Selection ICES 402, Paper 158 Madeleine Oliver, Emma Quick, Dana Masangkay, Isabella LeJeune-Bolivar, Lawrence Barrett, & Bruce Conger Amentum, Houston, TX Cinda Chullen, Colin Campbell, & Ryan Ogilvie NASA, Houston, TX 55th International Conference on Environmental Systems, Rio Grande, Puerto Rico, 12-16 July 2026

Portable Life Support System (PLSS) 2 • The PLSS supports extravehicular activities (EVAs) through 8 major functions • Oxygen storage and supply : Gaseous oxygen (GOX) • Ventilation : Liquid cooling ventilation garment (LCVG) • Flow drive : Centrifugal fans (vent loop) & pumps (water loop) • Carbon dioxide removal : Rapid cycle amine (RCA) • Humidity removal : Rapid cycle amine (RCA) • Thermal control : Spacesuit water membrane evaporator (SWME) • Trace contaminant control : Activated charcoal beds • Power and energy storage : Lithium-ion batteries • PLSS schematic studies have guided PLSS technology development and PLSS designs since the Apollo program, identifying the best path forward each time • In the early 2000s, the Constellation Space Suit Element PLSS schematic study was conducted, resulting in what is now the Exploration PLSS (xPLSS) • To achieve Mars surface exploration, modifications to the current xPLSS must be made • This schematic study investigates promising technologies for all major functions of the PLSS • Providing schematic recommendations for the Mars exploration PLSS (MxPLSS)

The Martian Environment 3 • There is an atmosphere with low pressure – no longer at vacuum conditions • Martian atmosphere is 95% CO2 at ~0.15 psia • Precludes use of venting technologies (SWME and RCA) without modification and calls for adjustments to suit insulation (gaseous atmosphere adds significant thermal conductance) • Martian gravity is ~2.5x lunar gravity • Martian gravity is 0.38g compared to Lunar gravity at 0.16g • On-back weight limits will be much more restrictive • Large travel distance and long mission duration • High reliability and regenerable elements to reduce weight and volume are necessary • Mars has seasonal changes/weather patterns or conditions • Materials used must withstand radiation received from planet and varying environmental conditions • Conditions such as dust, lighting, and visibility • Atmosphere introduces dust as a major hazard which could enter the space suit and expose CM to toxic particles – less abrasive than lunar soil but more reactive

FY24 Mars Schematic Study 4 • Blank-sheet approach was taken to compile a list of promising technologies that could satisfy the eight major functions of the PLSS • Initial list of 89 independent technologies which was reduced to 57 after Subject Matter Expert (SME) consultation • Developed mxPLSS specifications/requirements & assessment criteria • Environmental conditions, metabolic profiles, figures of merit, operational concepts, etc. • Guided Utility Sizer (GUS) tool developed to assess technologies and identify favorable schematics • Performs mass and heat balances to determine sizing and performance parameters for selected schematic combinations based on user defined inputs Function # of Technologies Considered Oxygen storage and supply 8 Ventilation network 2 Flow drive 6 Carbon dioxide removal* 22 Humidity removal* 25 Thermal control* 18 Trace contaminant control* 8 Power and energy storage 19 Total independent technologies 89 Eliminated -32 Technologies remaining 57 • Schematic down-selection conducted via Equivalent System Mass (ESM) analysis • Resulted in 7 PLSS schematic recommendations

Guided Utility Sizer (GUS) Tool 5 • A simplified, user-friendly sizing tool that performs mass and heat balances for user-selected PLSS schematics under a user-defined environment • Programmed within Microsoft Excel 2024 • Computes mass, power, volume and consumables requirements for selected technologies & associated PLSS • Includes sizing of relevant technologies modeled previously, as well as 24 new technology options never sized before • Mass balances for new technologies use experimental sizing data in literature & are correlated to PLSS operational requirements when necessary • Programmed to allow schematic sizing under a variety of operating conditions including Lunar and Mars environments, with refined calculations for evaluating convective heat transfer contributions on Mars

Major Upgrades to GUS 6 • The following upgrades were incorporated into GUS in FY25 to improve upon initial simplifications: • Addition and modification of previously existing technologies to maintain relevancy to the state of the art • Addition of secondary subsystem sizing as well as open & closed loop schematic configurations • Habitat/lander mass and architecture penalties for system-level assessment of schematics, including pre- and post- EVA consumables calculations • Enablement of transient heat balance analyses for selected PLSS schematics to increase fidelity of EVA evaluations in various environments • Improved tailoring to Mars missions via addition of location-specific Martian environments • With these upgrades, a higher-fidelity schematic analysis was performed that incorporates: • Primary and secondary subsystem contributions • System-level assessments of technology impacts on the vehicle level • Different system architectures investigated at different EVA times

Schematic Down-Selection 7 • Improved upon the fidelity of the previous schematic down selection process by using GUS to evaluate every possible schematic combination • Combinatorial process achieved using Mission Analysis and Integration Tool (MAIT) • Given a list of input and output variables, MAIT opened the GUS tool, plugged in technology options for each PLSS major function, and extracted calculated sizing and performance parameters for thousands of architectures at varying EVA times • Constraints and assumptions were implemented to reduce processing time by skipping incompatible or redundant schematic pairings • Results were sorted and postprocessed to determine lowest PLSS mass and vehicle mass options • PLSS options optimized for open loop, semi-open loop, and closed loop primary subsystem configurations at 2-, 4-, 6-, and 8-hour EVA durations • Secondary subsystem configuration always treated as open loop and is sized to operate for a duration of 0.5 hours with a 2-hour EVA and 1 hour with 4-, 6-, and 8-hour EVAs • For each case, the lowest mass options using both gaseous (GOX) and liquid (LOX) oxygen were recommended • A mass packaging factor of 2.32 and a volume packaging factor of 2.62 were applied to all schematics to get total PLSS mass and volume • A handful of architectures that optimize vehicle ESM were also considered

Operational & Environmental Parameters 8 • Primary Avg Met Rate : 350 W (1194 BTU/hr) • Primary Max Met Rate : 530 W (1810 BTU/hr) • Secondary Avg Met Rate : 295 W (1007 BTU/hr) • Secondary Max Met Rate : 350 W (1194 BTU/hr) • Suit Pressure : 4.3 psia • Inner Suit Temp : 294.3 K (70 F) • Primary EVA Time : 2, 4, 6, & 8 hours • Secondary EVA Time : 0.5, 1, 1, & 1 hour • Pre/post EVA duration : 2 hours • Mission Duration : 180 days • EVAs Scheduled : 100 • EVAs Contingency : 1 • Recharge Duration : 34 hours • EVA Crew : 2 Environment Surface Temp (K) Sky Temp (K) Atm. Assumptions 9 • LOX schematics • Primary subsystem – LOX is modeled with a ventilation heat exchanger and heater for vaporization (depending on schematic) • Secondary subsystem – LOX is modeled in conjunction with a super ice phase change material (PCM) as a vaporizer • GOX schematics • Modeled with a regulator in both primary and secondary subsystems • All recommended schematics • LCVG for ventilation network • Fan or ejector for ventilation flow drive • Pump for primary and secondary thermal loop flow drive • Sub-cooled PCM or radiator for secondary thermal control • Solid-state battery for primary and secondary power supply

Conclusions 15 • Lowest mass options vary based on EVA time • Shorter EVA times (2 & 4 hours): semi-open loop LOX, cryogenic scrubber, SWME + VP or VE EC radiator/SWME attachment • Longer EVA times (6 & 8 hours): closed loop LOX, LiOH/CHXR, upsized SWME • Some schematics that are not the lowest mass option within their own configuration category (closed, open, or semi-open loop) trade better than options in other categories • 8-hour EVA schematics optimized for vehicle ESM in the semi-open and closed loop configurations trade better than the option optimized for PLSS mass in the open loop configuration • Additional low mass options in each configuration category are being investigated in forward work Schematic Primary Subsystems Mass (kg) Vehicle ESM (kg) 1 Closed LOX + heater, fan + pump, LiOH, CHXR, SWME, activated charcoal 74.6 2441 2* Semi- Open LOX + heater, fan + vent HX + pump, RCA + BC, radiator + HP, nanoporous silica 86.4 466 3 Semi- Open LOX, ejector + pump, dual cryogenic scrubber, VE EC radiator, SWME topping unit, activated charcoal 87.4 3970 4* Closed LOX + heater, fan + vent HX + pump, HFM, radiator + HP, activated charcoal 90.5 498 5 Open LOX + vent HX + heater, pump, SWME 93.0 3698 6* Open LOX + vent HX + heater, pump, radiator + HP 95.6 2222 7 Closed GOX + regulator, fan + pump, LiOH, CHXR, SWME, activated charcoal 98.6 3374 8 Semi- Open GOX + regulator, ejector + pump, RCA + SG, SWME, nanoporous silica 110.8 3264 9 Open GOX + regulator, pump, SWME + VP 152.6 6931 *Low vehicle ESM option
